Yesterday I tried to do some interior design on a floor plan of an apt using ChatGPT, Grok and Claude. I had this idea about tearing down some interior walls, re-splitting the space, and expanding the bathroom with a walk-in closet attached to a master bedroom.

ChatGPT struggled mightily with respecting the physical dimensions of the floor layouts and kept trying to design floor space outside the physical boundaries of the building. But it was very eager to provide me with pretty visualizations.

Grok also struggled with correctly recognizing the dimensions of the space. It kept insisting that the dimensions were 10’x5’4” instead of 10’x10’ bc it was getting confused by markings of dimensions elsewhere (kitchen) on the floor plan.

Finally, out of frustrations of not getting very good results with either ChatGPT 6 Pro and Grok 4.6 Expert, I resorted to throwing the problem at Claude Opus 5.5 medium thinking that it was prob going to similarly disappoint bc historically I never associated Claude with image/visuals as much as code. 

Shockingly, Opus 5.5 nailed it out of the gate by doing a light schematic first and then upon promoting made a floor plan that respected the dimensions quite faithfully. Finally, when I asked for visualization, it created a 3D rendering of the space with different vantage angles for me to play around. I was deeply impressed.

This experience reminded me of the time maybe 6-12 months ago when Claude was beating everyone else at coding by just getting it right or one-shotting it. I’m sure there are ways in which I could’ve prompted ChatGPT/Grok to get a similarly good experience but this was my actual lived experience.

ChatGPT and Grok each displayed serious space hallucination problems while Claude was able to get it right immediately without repeated instructions of corrections and still failing. None of them displayed what I considered AGI, but Claude came closest. 

Despite clear rapid progress from the other labs and Claude genuinely becoming annoying in the way it talks, when it matters Claude still seems to have got it. That research taste edge seems very real. Others can grind harder, but Anthropic has that je ne sais quois. 

Anecdotal evidence. Not meant to be taken as universal whatsoever. Most likely a “skills issue” and it so happened that Claude didn’t require as much skill. But I thought it’s interesting to share esp in light of recent news of OpenAI pausing training of frontier models due to safety concerns.

AI progress has been extremely rapid but also highly uneven. AI models are still quite lacking in key dimensions but have already become extremely advanced at say coding and hacking to do serious damage. 

Leading labs will have to contend with the challenge of training generalist foundational models to further improve on the still lacking areas while controlling the dangerous arm so it doesn’t do (too much) damage. 

AI safety and alignment are real issues and an essential part of the input into the AI development process and not a nice-to-have afterthought. They are part of the “alpha”. If a lab cannot properly and efficiently manage safety/alignment, they could be stopped in their tracks and thwarted from progressing towards AGI/ASI fearing the liabilities of damage caused along the way. 

Maybe this is obvious to everyone but I hadn’t thought of it this way until recently.

This chart does not show an agentic bank run; it shows the collapse of cheap funding for banks.

This means return on equity for banks will collapse, as it will for brokers like Schwab and IBKR, where idle cash sitting in sweep accounts comprise something like half of their net revenues.

Business models built on friction and human laziness will (rightly!) get slaughtered in the coming years.

That said, agentic bank runs are another thing entirely, and they will absolutely happen. Remember, SVB was triggered by a fear contagion where all of their customers behaved the same way and triggered a stampede. Agents will be like this, but on steroids. 

The reason why agents magnify this kind of phenomenon is because AIs have much lower diversity of behavior than humans. This is especially true if we're all using the same model, like if everyone has Muse or Claude optimizing their finances.

See examples of this from the Anthropic research piece on multiagent systems. When you have multiple agents coordinating together in a game, you see a lot of bunching of behavior, and very little strategic diversity compared to humans.

This means cascading agentic bank runs will likely be more violent and sudden than human ones. The banking system is absolutely not ready for this.

US bond market volatility is at historic levels.

The MOVE index jumped +19% last week, its largest weekly increase since April 2025, following "Liberation Day."

This index is also called the "VIX of bonds" and measures the yield volatility of 2Y, 5Y, 10Y, and 30Y Treasuries.

This marks its 3rd-largest weekly increase since the 2022 bear market.

The move comes as the 10Y Note Yield jumped +17 basis points last week, to 5.17%, its highest level since June 2007.

At the same time, the 30Y Note Yield rose +16 basis points and surpassed 5.50% for the first time since June 2004.

To put this into perspective, in the week ending March 17th, 2023, the MOVE Index surged +29% following the US banking crisis, when 3 regional banks collapsed.

The US Treasury market is experiencing crisis-like volatility.

AI is changing how content gets written and who it’s written for.

This already happened once with Google, and I can see the same thing starting with AI search.

@Semrush compared 300K+ URLs cited by AI with pages ranking on Google. AI-cited pages were much more likely to use:

→ Clear summaries
→ Q&A formatting
→ Structured sections
→ Other formats that make information easier for models to extract

Clear summarization showed the biggest gap at 32.83%.

And this is where I think it gets unhealthy.

Once AI citations become valuable distribution, publishers have a reason to structure content around what ChatGPT, Gemini, or Perplexity can easily pick up instead of what the reader finds helpful.

So the quality of that content will probably shift too.

We already know what happened when everyone started writing for Google instead of readers. Pages became longer, more formulaic, and less useful.

Probably why genuinely good content is so hard to find now.

🗡️ What DeFi Shipped 🚢 (Sept 25):

Nasdaq approved Pyth to distribute its stock-price data, Ondo added a way to tokenize existing shares, and Hyperliquid switched on borrowing.

Here’s how those work, plus 7 more updates worth catching up on:

• @HyperliquidX turned on manual borrows. You can now post HYPE or BTC as collateral and borrow USDC or USDT, with rates set by utilization.

• @Ondo now lets approved institutions mint Ondo Stocks with shares they already hold, through @AlpacaHQ's Instant Tokenization Network. It's live on Ethereum and @BNBCHAIN.

• @PythNetwork won Nasdaq approval to redistribute Nasdaq Basic through its data feeds. That puts licensed US equity prices on the same rails as its crypto feeds.

• @Polymarket hired Zora's former CEO Jacob Horne to "make Polymarket DeFi great again." @shayne_coplan admits the onchain product has waned while the team focused on the US.

• @zetachain holders voted to migrate ZETA to Solana, with 99.4% in favor. The team is folding its L1 and betting everything on @anumaai, its private AI app.

• @stablecoin_x's 48-month lock-up on its ENA is permanently waived from October 5. Its stack is ~3.03B ENA, about 20% of supply, although any sale still needs @ethena Foundation consent.

• @variational_io says its $VAR TGE will occur in Q4 2026, with 32% of the total supply airdropped to users based on Variational points.

• @jumperapp is getting a token. solana:Aybt5BWuW6kMNt7Jk1UmSgLzpEKev5pEnh82TA5rpump was announced days after a perps waitlist went up.

• @Trueo_ is moving its prediction market from @base to Ethereum mainnet, pointing to deeper integrations and its next oracle system. TRUE holders can migrate with no deadline.

• @longdotxyz says it will act as an incubator, not a launcher, working with top stock-pair teams to build their own moats. Stricter "PVE" protections like ticker locks are coming too.

An L1 voted itself out of existence, and a prediction market is leaving Base for Ethereum mainnet. 

Nobody's loyal to infrastructure anymore, esp when it's so easy to bridge and shift tokens around. 

They go wherever the users and the liquidity already are.

Bitcoin closed above the May high, which is technically a point for the bulls, and the burden of proof remains with the bears to prove otherwise.

Given that BTC is still <1% away from the May high, it makes it hard to jump to conclusions going into Q4 (as much as I would like to do so). I thought that maybe by now it would either have accepted back below or be much higher, but instead price has barely moved.

Usually after passing the 50W like in 2019/2023, BTC then runs 20-30% within 1-2 weeks. This time, the move has been much more muted, probably because of fears over seasonality and yields heading higher (which is often bearish for long-duration assets like crypto).

Kind of a frustrating time to be honest, because on one hand what makes sense to me would be weakness into Q4, but BTC continues to show strength, making me sincerely question that view. And historically, the weakness often starts before Q4 arrives (which it has not yet so far this time). 

I suppose I should be less deterministic about my views going forward, as this whole move has been extremely humbling.

Mario Bros was just a classic. first game i played on my NES. game with Duck Hunt and the zapper and i got the one with the Power Pad bundled in with World Class Track Meet

Zelda was the first open world exploration game i (and most other people) had ever played. so many secrets on the map that we used to scour strategy guides and discuss it with friends at school. tried bombing every wall in every dungeon

Mega Man 3 didn't invent the formula, but it basically perfected it. the graphics and soundtrack and bosses were just peak

Civilization 1 was probably the first serious strategy game i played on the family's 286 PC. Civ 2 would eventually be a big leap, but 1 was truly epic for the time. really felt like you were managing an empire and piqued my interest in places around the world

Sim City 1 on PC was an epic management simulator. it is probably still better than most city builder shovel ware on mobile app stores. had to really manage a budget to make it work

Streets of Rage 2 was the quintessential beat 'em up brawler. amazing graphics and soundtrack. one of the most fun games you could get together with your friends and just play. closet thing we had to Final Fight at home

Warcraft II was real-time strategy basically perfected, with an engaging story and characters and art style to boot. but what made this one shine was playing it with friends (modem to modem), and later with IPX over TCP/IP tools like Kali. absolutely crazy experience playing this thing on the internet with other people

Quake is probably the greatest FPS ever created. fully unlocked camera. felt like it came from the future. and running GL Quake with a Monster 3D or similar graphics card was a defining experience. rich online IRC and web communities. amazing mods like CTF and Team Fortress. no other shooter since has done what this one did for me

Diablo defined the ARPG genre. While Diablo 2 perfected it, Diablo 1 was absolutely ground breaking. i remember my first playthrough of this one more than i do many other games (and remember trading an item with someone online i met in a lobby who quickly stole my item and killed me)

anyways, once every cycle there comes a product that is incredibly K-shaped with many losers and few winners.

it is ironic and poetic that this comes from the space with the most K-shaped outcomes, fuelled by people who want to get out of the lower income bracket into the upper income bracket, but they choose to do so by playing games that inherently favor a large amount of losers vs a small amount of winners. 

basically, it's like going to the casino in order to get rich. i used to get upset as well over this sort of thing, but over time, after seeing this play out every cycle, with first NFTs, then memecoins, then exchanges, then now fomo, i have come to appreciate the Matt Levine stance on this. It goes something like this:

https://t.co/XYdbmA8nse
"
1. Anyone can invest all they want in a diversified portfolio of approved investments (non-penny-stock public companies, mutual funds and exchange-traded funds with modest fees, insured bank accounts, etc.).

2. Anyone can also invest in any other dumb investment; you just have to go to the local office of the SEC and get a Certificate of Dumb Investment. (Anyone who sells dumb non-approved investments without requiring this certificate from buyers goes to prison.)

3. To get that certificate, you sign a form. The form is one page with a lot of white space. It says in very large letters: “I want to buy a dumb investment. I understand that the person selling it will almost certainly steal all my money, and that I would almost certainly be better off just buying index funds, but I want to do this dumb thing anyway. I agree that I will never, under any circumstances, complain to anyone when this investment inevitably goes wrong. I understand that violating this agreement is a felony.”

4. Then you take the form to an SEC employee, who slaps you hard across the face and says “really???” And if you reply “yes really” then she gives you the certificate.
